utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony, to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just a second. Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just like yesterday, could you please take care that we do not overlap when speaking.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The last topic we dealt with yesterday was the Vance Plan. You spoke about the meeting that you attended, the meeting between late Mr. Babic with Mr. Vance. Can you tell us whether you are aware of the reason why Mr. Babic asked for Mr. Vance that UN troops be deployed according to the ink blocks, ink blot system in towns outside the territory of the urban communities.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Babic explained to Mr. Vance. The point was that Serbs in Croatia's cities and towns were already subjected to mass dismissals, that some executions of Serbs had already begun, and that they were in jeopardy. Mr. Babic guaranteed to Mr. Vance complete safety for Croats in the territory of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, I must add, I'm sorry, that Mr. Babic suggested, after that, that UN troops be deployed on the line of separation, on the demarcation line. Mr. Vance would not even talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I asked you yesterday, when a lawyer says "thank you," you stop. Will you please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, thank you, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please may I just ask the witness. Witness, what do you mean by "execution of Serbs"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, by that time we already had reports that Serbs were being killed in Croatia's towns and cities, that is something that people knew and stories about that circulated among the people. We had no official data, but we knew that that was going on. And later on those reports proved true and even films were made about it. Croats did it later in Karlovac, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You used the word "executions" for this. Why did you use this word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, if you take somebody, for instance, to Maska Poljana, that is Manja field, or maybe that is not the name, I can't remember now. You take them from their home and the person never comes back, you reckon that they were executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What are you referring to? Just in one sentence, please. I said just in one sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If somebody is taken away from their home and never comes back then you reckon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You are a witness and you should tell us about facts and to what facts did you refer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was reported by all the newspapers, for instance, is one case in Zagreb where the whole family named Zec was killed off. It was in all the newspapers. In Krajina such things did not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr. Milovancevic, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Babic told Mr. Vance the reasons why he was asking for UN troops to be deployed across Croatia's towns and cities to protect the Serbs, did he familiarise Mr. Vance with some of the reports and information? Did he explain why he was asking for that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Babic did explain certainly why he was asking that. I can't remember the details, but he certainly had his reasons for making that demand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember that you said you had been to Geneva with Mr. Babic in early 1991 at talks where the party armed forces of the HDZ were discussed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We went to Geneva to make our case before the United Nations, meaning to ask protection from the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see on the screen Exhibit 36 or a document from the Prosecution 65 ter list 1226.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe it is Exhibit 236, if that is helpful. 65 ter number 1226 is Exhibit 236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the left top corner. Can you see, Witness, this document?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What does it seem to be about?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only read the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I meant. Could you please read to us the heading and the title.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina. The government of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knin, 5th September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see to whom the document was sent?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The peace conference of -- on Yugoslavia in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 7 in B/C/S. That is marked 4834 in the right top corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this document being sent to the peace conference of Yugoslavia in The Hague as the witness says? Or is it being sent to the SFRY Presidency offices?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not ask the witness to whom it was sent. I just asked him who seems to be the addressee from the heading of the document. I just wanted him to read what is written on the document itself, and the question you raised is one we were about to deal with right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the question I raised is already on the transcript at page 4, line 25. Do you see? To whom the document was sent? It may have been an interpretation problem, but I think, then, if we can just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was not a misinterpretation. I asked the question in such a way that it gives rise, indeed, to the question you asked. But, in fact, I wanted the witness just to tell us to whom the letter was addressed. And if you allow me, I will ask the witness. Can we see from the cover page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To whom -- for whom it was meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it addressed to the peace conference? Or is the subject the peace conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is written on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry. You were asked a question with "or." So the answer "yes" is not very clear, is it? To whom was this letter supposed to be sent? It's according to what is written on the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite clear from the text that it was addressed to the peace conference in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Where do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, it's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is written in the heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Heading and addressee, this is two different things, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion between the title of the letter or what I would refer to as the caption, the subject matter of the letter and the person to whom the letter is addressed. I think all of the Judges have a different person as the addressee of the letter than what the witness has said, and that's a material point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I will try, through questions to the witness, without any explanations of my own, to get at that. Since we are seeing on the monitor the page that we have here, I would like to continue and I believe we will reach an answer to your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed. Did you say we must go to page 7 of the B/C/S? What page in the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know the number of that page, but it's the last page of this document bearing a stamp. So the very end of that document, and on that page we see who signed it, together with the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on the seventh page of the document in B/C/S, we see something in the bottom right corner, if we can zoom in on it, please.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it even without zooming in. It says: "Head of the government of SAO Krajina, Dr. Milan Babic." And from the contents of the letter, it is obvious that it is addressed to the peace conference in The Hague. That is what the contents tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 8 in B/C/S where we can see to whom the letter was delivered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a moment. Do you see there is no peace conference in The Hague amongst the people to whom it is sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will get an answer even to that question now, Your Honour. We will ask the witness what he knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is written on this Page 8, to whom was the letter delivered?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, to the United Nations. Two, to the Ministerial Council of the European Community. Three, to the parliament of the European Community. Four, to the High Commission of the OSCE. The conference in European Cooperation and Security. Five, to the Presidency of the SFRY. Six, to the Federal Executive Council. Seven, to the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia. Eight, to the President of the Republic of Serbia. Seven, to the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now go back to page 1. The last four digits of the ERN number are 4828. You said a while ago, while reading the left top, left-hand top corner, saying who composed this letter, you said that. And when I asked you whom it was addressed to you said something. Could you take another look at this title and say whether it can be concluded to whom it is addressed.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says in the title: "The peace conference on Yugoslavia in The Hague," meaning that it is to be the recipient of that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the first paragraph of this letter, just below the title.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government of the Serbian Autonomous District of the Krajina, at a session held on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Neither can the interpreter ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we just look at the first paragraph. Scroll down please to the beginning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government of the Serbian Autonomous District of the Krajina, at a session held on the 5th of September, 1991, discussed the declaration on Yugoslavia adopted at the extraordinary ministerial meeting of the European political community in Brussels on the 27th of August, 1991. A cease-fire agreement and a memorandum on an observer mission, and in that connection adopted the following stances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know about the existence of this letter before I showed it to you today?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that Mr. Babic sent to international organisations I had to translate into English. Of course I cannot remember all the details of all of that correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's your answer to the question? The question was: "Did you know about the existence of this letter before I showed it to you today."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I haven't got used to this procedure. Okay, sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And you mean you know the contents already when looking at the first page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there have been so many. No, that is not what I mean. I translated all the documents into the English language, and I certainly cannot recall them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No. I was asking you, you before said, I think, from the contents you can tell immediately to whom this letter was addressed. And only later we found out that at the end it was said that to eight addressees it was addressed. And the heading The Hague Peace Conference in Yugoslavia has apparently not directly to do with the question to whom the letter was addressed. So don't you agree? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So you may conclude that your idea was a little premature when saying it's quite clear? Please, so don't make any premature conclusions. Just say step by step what you are being asked. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought the evidence has revealed that there was one addressee, but in fact a number of deliverees [Realtime transcript read in error "deliveries"]. It was addressed to a particular person and then delivered and copied to a number of others. Yes. Please go ahead, Mr. Milovancevic. If Judge Hoepfel has finished?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, at the very beginning when I presented this document to you, I asked you what was written in the top left-hand corner. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You read out that the letter was sent, being sent by the government of the SAO Krajina. Then I asked you to whom it was addressed. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I read out the title believing that it was to reach that conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you read out -- read that title, were you interpreting what was written in the content or did you just read the title?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just read the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, when we have shown to you both the first and last pages and the addresses to which the letter was sent, what is your position about this letter in view of the existing title? To whom was it written basically?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- you can see the addresses to which it is addressed, but it was certainly to be at the peace conference in The Hague for the people there to be informed of its content. That is also obvious from the content which asks the peace conference to provide the protection that we refer to. It is not the other addressees that are asked for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Just before you go on. I would just like to make a correction of the record at page 10, line 7. The third word from the end should be "deliverees," e-e-s on the end. Subjective, the person to whom it was delivered. Not "deliveries" the noun, the object. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, whether in September 1991 a peace conference was being held in The Hague, a peace conference on Yugoslavia was being held in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who had convened that conference, which countries, and what was the subject of it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not exactly enumerate the bodies. I believe at any rate it was the European Community. It was her department, and I believe it was called the European Community at that particular point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now take a look at the second page of this letter in B/C/S, the -- marked as 4829 in the B/C/S. And I wish to finish with this document. Can you read for us the second paragraph from the top, Mr. Macura.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not see it on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll down so that the second paragraph from the top would appear on the screen. You should scroll down, actually.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be scrolled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you see, Mr. Macura.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have page number 2, the second paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second paragraph from the top? I can read it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, do.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Croatian neo-fascist authorities, in certain elements identical to the former communist totalitarianism sought by bringing Yugoslavia down, to force us to reconcile ourselves to terror and not to apply what Croatia views as its natural right, the right to self-determination, up to secession. Under such circumstances, with being" -- can you scroll it down a bit please, a bit more, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is asking for the text to be scrolled down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "...in such circumstances where there are challenging of a referenda of our equal right, we had no option but to respond by arms, with arms to arms. The new Croatia -- the new Croatia attacked a right in our decisions with weapons in the intention of forcing by aggression the Serbian people to live in independent neo-fascist Croatian state, a state so reminiscent of" -- can you scroll the text down, please -- "and not only to us Serbs of that genocidal time," the years 1941 to 1945 are indicated there in brackets, "when it was also called and comported itself in," in inverted commas, "independent, or independently, from any common sense and humanity."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says in the introductory part, I mean the title of that, this was the position adopted at the session of the government of the SAO Krajina as regards the situation and the peace conference in Yugoslavia. Was Mr. Babic -- did Mr. Babic share these standpoints of the government which he actually signed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now remove this document from the monitor. I thank you. What happened -- what became of the talks with Mr. Vance? Seeing that he wouldn't accommodate the request of Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He, Mr. Vance, actually seeing that the situation with Mr. Babic was like that, opted for exerting pressure on the president of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic. After that, the government of the Krajina was dismantled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that after that Mr. Vance went to exert pressure on Mr. Milosevic, do you know or can you tell us what does that mean, to exert pressure how and with what objective in mind?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the objective of having the Vance Plan accepted unconditionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in connection with the acceptance of that plan, there was a Presidency session held in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a session of the Presidency held, and I attended it, as did -- there were a number of us from the Krajina attending it. Members of the government and the municipality presidents from the Krajina attended the session. Also, representatives of Serbs from Bosnia were there with Dr. Radovan Karadzic at the helm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where was this meeting held and who organised it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I don't know who organised the meeting, but we were driven, taken by car into a space, a big conference room. I don't remember the exact circumstances. I know that, for instance, Petar Stikovac fainted and Dr. Karadzic attended to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with this answer of yours, please tell us whether any of the members of the Presidency attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was indeed organised by the Presidency of Yugoslavia, because President Jovic was there, as were Generals Adzic and Kukanjac, and they were all exerting pressure on us, telling us that we had to accept the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was their explanation, what reasons did they give you for that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that it was a quite unpleasant meeting because they were shouting, especially General Adzic was shouting at us, calling us from the Krajina all sorts of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a question. Do you say you don't know where. You can't tell us which town this meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in Belgrade. I just do not remember the exact conference venue, because I don't know Belgrade that well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. At least that gives some kind of answer to the question: "Where was the meeting held and do you know who organised it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What were the arguments that were adduced to substantiate the Presidency's and the Generals' request to you to accept the plan? What was their argumentation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their arguments were that we would be completely protected by the Vance Plan, whereas we claimed the opposite, and regrettably that was proven true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Macura, their argumentation was that "we would be completely protected by the Vance Plan." Who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs in the Krajina. General Adzic and Mr. Jovic guaranteed that the JNA would be the guarantor of our protection, and we said that they would not even be in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you -- did they tell you why the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Mr. Jovic, and General Adzic, did they tell you why they thought it would be good for the -- for the United Nations troops to come? What did they tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you that they asserted that the JNA was present and would remain in the Krajina, but nothing came of it, and they said: We remain in Bosnia and we are in Grahovo, and Grahovo is just ten minutes from Knin by car, and we told them: You won't be even in Bosnia because you will have to leave Bosnia as well. And then General Adzic was angry, and so was Mr. Jovic, and they claimed that they would never be leaving Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned Bosnia, what was Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia was one of the republics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why do you say that Mr. Jovic and General Adzic told you that they would be in Bosnia? Who is "they" and why in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He meant Yugoslav People's Army, because this was war. So, therefore, and why they thought that they would be in Bosnia, I don't know that. That is a question you should be asking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was any reference at all at the time made to the possibility of Bosnia's secession and Bosnia's independence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody referred to that at that time at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But did it occur afterwards?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When, Mr. Macura?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very soon thereafter. I don't know the date. I do apologise. Perhaps I should have recorded dates, but I didn't. I know that Bosnia recognised why the war was still on as, after all was Croatia, was recognised while the combat operations was still going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the -- Mr. Jovic and General Adzic, in addition to this immediate task of, as you call it, the protection of the Serbs in the Krajina, did they also tell you why they thought that peace operation important for Yugoslavia and why it should be accepted generally? What were their political arguments, not only talking about the factual situation.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat what General Adzic said. He said that -- he actually didn't use very polished language, if I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can say it in a decent way.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said: "You bandits from the Krajina cannot take an entire state for a ride, you know." "You riff-raff from Knin." That is what he said to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So that is the attitude of General Adzic to the Serbs from the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was he, what is he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that one of the participants in the meeting from Krajina fainted. Why?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Mr. Pero Stikovac, who was a professor. And why he fainted, I think simply because it was a very, very difficult situation. He could not endure it. He started quarrelling with Mr. -- General Adzic, and he grabbed him, physically assaulted him, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General Adzic held a post at that time. What was he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Yugoslav army, of the JNA. Or the commander of the General Staff. I am not sure what the designation is, but he was the person, the chief in command of the Yugoslav army at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the Vance Plan accepted after all that, and how?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Vance Plan was adopted when, in Glina, a town in Krajina, a meeting or a session was held of the Assembly of SAO Krajina which was illegal. They simply assembled people according to their own selection. Very few of them were members of the Assembly. Branko Kostic attended this meeting as well. At the time he was the president of the Presidency, of the rump Yugoslavia as it was called. So at this Assembly, the government of Milan Babic was, in fact, toppled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the Vance Plan adopted?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later on it was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any explanation put forward on why the Vance Plan should be adopted? I'm referring to the attitude of the politicians in Krajina; there were probably some differences of opinion.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was among those who opposed the adoption of the Vance Plan. I translated the entire plan for Babic, from English. We were going around Krajina canvassing and holding rallies, where we tried to explain why this plan should not be adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Macura, could you tell us very briefly what was the essence of your opposition to this plan. The war, the secession, annexation, what was the exact reason?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believed that this was tantamount to an occupation of the Krajina region. And we thought that the United Nations served only as a means to defend, for Croatia to be able to accomplish all its objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this, in fact, so?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why are you saying this?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is very clear from this point in time, because right now they're only elderly people living in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the goal of Jovic and Adzic was for the Serbs to flee this region?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard what Stipe Mesic said in connection to Bora Jovic when he was asked about the situation of Serbs in the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bora Jovic said that as far as they were concerned, they could do whatever they wanted with the Serbs. You can do whatever you want with them, we don't care.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this the support that you received from Belgrade in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. But I can't add anything, not to -- in order not to irritate the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You don't have to take the Bench's feelings into account. Tell us the truth as you know it. Whether the Bench is irritated or not, it is not for you to tell. And I don't know how you would know the Bench would be irritated. Just say what you want to say without concerning yourself with how the Bench will react.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you wish to go ahead and tell us then what you held back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovic said -- can even impale them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Jovic convicted before this -- indicted before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But he was the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until when did you hold the post of the minister of information?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the Glina Assembly that was held illegally. The entire government was dismissed then, and then Mr. Zecevic formed a new government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with Z-4 plan? Do you know what it refers to?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Z-4 plan was the plan of Croatia for the autonomy of Serbs within Croatia, and in fact this autonomy referred to the district of Glina and the district of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for interrupting you. I will let you finish this sentence, but I wanted to ask you why you said that the Z-4 was a Croatian plan, the plan of the Croatian state and not of the international community.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the plan devised by Croatia and was supposed to be implemented by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what was the reaction of Mr. Martic as the president of Krajina or when this plan was put forward to him?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was on the Knin fortress. Mr. Martic asked for guarantees for the UNPROFOR mandate to be extended. Since Croatia had already announced that it would not be in favour of this extension of the UNPROFOR mandate, and since he did not receive guarantees that the mandate would be extended, Mr. Martic did not want to discuss the plan, nor to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with Mr. Galbraith's name?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the ambassador of the United States in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did he have anything to do with the Z-4 plan? Mr. Galbraith, I mean.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly did, since he was the representative of the -- of the world superpower, which certainly affects everything that happens in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What does Operation Flash mean to you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the cleansing of Western Slavonia on the part of the Croatian police and army forces. They were trying to cleanse it from Serbs. I think this was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was Western Slavonia at the time under somebody's protection?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Western Slavonia was part of Krajina and was protected by the UN troops, by UNPROFOR troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After, as you referred to it, the cleansing of Western Slavonia by Croatian forces, did the representatives of Krajina take part into any subsequent meetings with the Croatian authorities, with respect to Krajina negotiations?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no further discussions. This was already dealt with in a military way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I refer to Geneva and I take you back to the beginning of August 1995, does it bring back anything?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We held negotiations. I was one of the participants of the negotiations on behalf of Krajina. We negotiated with the Croatian authorities, and this was under the chairmanship of Mr. Stoltenberg. In the morning, we met in a plenary session, both the Croatian side and ourselves, and later on Mr. Stoltenberg had a -- separate discussions with each of the delegations. In the course of these discussions that he held with us, we accepted all of his demands, all of Mr. Stoltenberg's demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you for a moment. When you said that you accepted all of his demands, are you referring to his own personal demands?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We thought that these were demands that were formulated by the United Nations, and were put forward to us by Mr. Stoltenberg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What exactly did you accept?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We agreed to guarantee the normal functioning throughout the territory of Croatia, would be restored all the tracks, the infrastructure, the roads, and the oil pipes. We also agreed that this should be completed on the ground in cooperation with the Croatian authorities within 15 days. The Croatian side demanded that we sign a capitulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. When was this requested by the Croatian authorities, before or after you accepted these demands?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we accepted the demands, at the morning session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you accept to capitulate?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said that we did not have the mandate to sign a capitulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But you said that you accepted all the demands put forward by Mr. Stoltenberg.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened on the 3rd of August, 1995, what happened subsequently?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening, I was invited by the representative of the Russian mission in Geneva, I was invited to a meeting and he told me that the United States and Germany gave a green light to Croatia to attack Krajina, and that they would be assisting them in this effort. And this is what happened at dawn of the next day, Krajina was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of this operation, of this attack on Krajina?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This operation was referred to as "Storm" and is now celebrated as the day of independence in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the Defence Exhibit 1D0130 shown on the screen, please. Zoom in on the photograph, please. Perfect. Can you recognise anyone on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Left, you can see Mr. Galbraith, the ambassador of the United States to Croatia, he was riding on a tank. And I heard his statement when he said that the Serbs occupied Croatia, whereas he himself was trying to expel Serbs from the territory that was inhabited by Serbs for hundreds of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, where was this taken, this photograph? What does it say beneath, underneath the photograph?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "on a Croatian tank." American Ambassador Galbraith. This was also on the TV, I saw it on TV. He was rushing people to go faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Rushing people? Which people?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian refugees who were expelled from their land.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, Mr. Galbraith testified here and claimed that he was never atop a Croatian tank.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not telling the truth. I saw this on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I believe that misstates the evidence. He didn't say he was never atop a Croatian tank. He said he wasn't on a Croatian tank in Operation Storm, and that is a critical difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has, to Mr. Galbraith as a protected witness and the former ambassador of the United States to Croatia, put the question whether he was photographed atop a Croatian tank. He answered that he didn't. When the question was put to him again, he gave an explanation that he was atop an American Chevrolet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't do it now, because I did not have this transcript, but my colleague from the Prosecution can confirm that he was not atop a Croatian tank and this is sufficient for me. If needed, I can look for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your learned friend from the Prosecution is objecting, and if you insist on what you are saying, you've got to refer us to a transcript, otherwise you will have to hang on before you can follow on this issue. Judge Hoepfel seems to have it somewhere. Let's find out from him. He might be able to help you. Yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: If you want to know, Mr. Milovancevic, it's transcript 3851, line 15. "Are you familiar with the fact," Mr. Galbraith was asked, "that the world media, that the world media published your photo on a tank of the Croatian army, a photo that was taken during Operation Storm?" Answer: "No photograph was taken of me during Operation Storm on a Croatian tank. I was not on a Croatian tank during Operation Storm." And so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Hoepfel. That is precisely what I meant, and that was the gist of my question to the witness. Therefore, Mr. Galbraith lied before this court, and he even deceived the Trial Chamber by saying he was atop a passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Objection. It is not at all the question that he had put before. It is quite different. And I object to this argument now on it. He can put to him what Mr. Galbraith said, if that is even proper under the guidelines that the Chamber has set forth, to ask for a comment of another witness, but what he can't do is misstate what Ambassador Galbraith said when he came to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, what you put to this witness is different from what he said -- what Judge Hoepfel read. Now I will ask you to say exactly what it is that you allege was put to Ambassador Galbraith and what his answer was. Can you just say what was put to him and what his answer was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, with pleasure. I asked the ambassador whether he was aware that the world media had published his photograph atop a Croatian tank during Operation Storm. I asked him that question maybe even twice, and Mr. Galbraith said he had not been on the Croatian tank but atop a vehicle belonging to the American embassy. Now we see his photograph atop a tank, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is not what his answer is here. His answer is he was never on top of a Croatian tank during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, but I asked him: Were you atop a Croatian tank during Operation Storm? And he said no. Now we see a photograph showing that, yes, he was. I don't understand the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Wait a minute, Mr. Milovancevic. You don't misrepresent the questions. What you are telling this witness is not -- unless what Judge Hoepfel was reading here is not what you were referring to when you were talking about the transcript, if you can show us some other part of the transcript, I will allow you to carry on. Otherwise I am afraid you are misrepresenting the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just add one point that I think is important. Unless I missed something, this does not say that this photograph was taken during Operation Storm. There is no indication of that on the caption that was read. It said Ambassador Galbraith up on a tank. Not that it was taken during Operation Storm. And I would note that this is also leading, because the witness -- this exact question was asked of the witness. It says: Mr. Macura, where was this taken, this photograph? And he says it was on a Croatian tank. He doesn't say anything about Operation Storm. But now if the next question was, was this taken during Operation Storm, well, the witness has been given an answer by Defence counsel through argumentative questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I just wondered, Mr. Black, if there is anything within the text itself that would shed light and would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid - sorry, Judge - that the witness is being asked about the picture, not about the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Milovancevic, I'm afraid you are misrepresenting the evidence and you are either going to stay away from that question, or you phrase it properly. The choice is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will reformulate my question. What matters to us is the essence, not the form. That is sometimes meant to hide the essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, Mr. Milovancevic, I rule that remark out of order, because we are all here looking for substance and not form. And the substance of the question, of the answer by Ambassador Galbraith on the transcript was he was never on a Croatian tank during Operation Storm. He doesn't say he was never on a tank, on a Croatian tank. He may have been on a Croatian tank some other time. But not during Operation Storm. If you cannot make that distinction, then don't make insinuations that you cannot substantiate. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this man, second to the right from Mr. Galbraith has a cap. Do you see any emblem on the cap?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to see the insignia, but it should be one of the Croatian officers. Who else could it be? Although the photograph is not the clearest, but this emblem on the cap is the chequer-board symbol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you are telling the witness that it is a chequer-board? He said he can't see. Now you're telling him what it is. You can see, you tell us why you say the chequer-board. You can take the witness stand and tell us why you say it is a chequer-board, because we don't see any chequer-board here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness answered literally that he saw the chequer-board. I will ask him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is time for our break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before we go, I'm not able to identify the tank. I think I am less technically minded than my brothers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I need assistance there. Probably when we come back, if not now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber will take -- I beg your pardon. The Court will take a short break. We will come back at quarter to 11.00, and we'll keep this photograph on the screen. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before the break, Judge Nosworthy was confessing her technical limitations and asking to be assisted to see the tank. I must confess, I happen to be in the same company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in e-court we have the same photograph of which we have a hard copy, and since the photo that we have on paper is clearer, I would like to distribute those copies, and then I would like to ask the witness some questions on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, pardon the interruption. There was some discussion between counsel over the break, and we were certainly under the impression that Defence counsel was going to correct some things that were incorrect that were said before the break, and I just wonder if Defence counsel is going to do that now. That's what I thought was going to happen, but I am just enquiring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe I interrupted because we opened this later session now with me talking first. Mr. Milovancevic, is there anything that you agreed with your opposite number during the break which you would like to place on the record before we go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Honourable Judge Hoepfel rightly indicated page 3851 where we have on record the question I asked of Witness Galbraith; namely, was he aware that the world media published his photo on the tank during Operation Storm, and his answer was that he had never been on a tank during Operation Storm. He was standing atop a tractor, or something. So his answer was he was never atop a Croatian tank during Operation Storm. And I think that was the question, the part of the record that is relevant both for the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber. So the -- my point is, I accept that this photograph is not from Operation Storm, because Ambassador Galbraith said he had never been atop a Croatian tank during Operation Storm. He later gave some additional explanations related to vehicles belonging to the American embassy and his personal vehicles, but in order to avoid reviewing the entire transcript, we have the photograph in front of us now and, with your leave, I would like to ask the question of the witness, what does he see on the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even before I ask Mr. Black to say what he wants to say, my question to you would be: If you accept, as you now seem to be saying, that Mr. Galbraith was never on a Croatian tank during Operation Storm, if you accept that, is this picture still relevant to the proceedings? Do we still need to talk about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do, very much so, because precisely on this photo Ambassador Galbraith is atop a tank, indeed. And he explained, during his testimony here, that he had been in contact with Mr. Tudjman sometime several times a day, and it is very important for the sake of establishing facts, to establish what exactly Mr. Galbraith did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand you. Now you are bringing Mr. Tudjman into the equation. Obviously we can talk about what Mr. Galbraith said and did with Mr. Tudjman, but unless you're saying that he's with Mr. Tudjman on the tank, and that's one of the things that you want to say he did with him, but I don't know whether we need this photograph to talk about what they did. The point of the matter is, if the question to him had been that he was on top of a tank during Operation Storm and he said, no, he was never on top of a tank during Operation Storm and that answer is accepted by the Defence, then my question of relevance becomes very important, because he's not denying that he was ever on top of a tank. But he only says he was never on top of a tank during Operation Storm. I don't know whether he was asked whether he was ever on top of a tank at all and he denied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Galbraith - and we can open this page 3851, line 5 and onwards - he did say he had never been atop a Croatian tank in Operation Storm. He was only on top of a tractor during Operation Flash, only a tractor, which shows that he denies he was ever on a tank. And in further discussion, when he was asked where he was at that moment, Mr. Galbraith explained that he was only on an armoured American vehicle; in fact, a bullet-proof vehicle of the American embassy. But what is important to me is not exactly that answer. It's the relevance of this topic, I have to tell you that. Why this photograph is relevant to me. Irrespective of when it was taken, it is important that the American ambassador is on top of a tank. What could an American ambassador be possibly doing atop a tank? He was a witness here and he testified and commented upon his earlier written reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But don't you think what you are doing is actually what you should be doing at the time of argument? I really think what you are now saying is appropriate at the time of argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this photograph is related to the text on the same page and it is relevant directly to the testimony of Witness Macura. After we establish who is on this photograph, I would like to put to this witness the text of this article related to Ambassador Galbraith and the negotiations in Geneva, a certain passage on this page consisting of only two brief sentences. All of this is directly relevant and related to the testimony of this witness. I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's your right. You are entitled to do that, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm sorry, I interrupted the translator. You can do that. All I'm asking you is what you are saying on whether or not Mr. Galbraith lied when he said he was never on a Croatian tank during Operation Storm, isn't that what you should be preserving for argument? The other things, you haven't gone to text yet, so I don't know what you are going to say about text and I am not commenting on the text. I am commenting on that statement only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You agree with that? Thank you very much. I don't know whether that dispenses with your -- what you were going to say when you stood up or you still have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I do still have something to say, Your Honour, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's just that in our view, Defence counsel has accepted the truth of what Ambassador Galbraith said, that he was not on a Croatian tank during Operation Storm, so I think when counsel said at page 25, line 19 that Ambassador Galbraith lied under oath, he should withdraw that comment. I'm not even sure that's the kind of thing that he should be making in argument. But separate from that distinction, I think that if he accepts the truth of what Mr. Galbraith said, then he should publicly withdraw his comment that he lied. It's on page 25 at line 19. And I quote: "Therefore, Mr. Galbraith lied before this court and he even deceived the Trial Chamber." Now, I don't think those kind of comments are appropriate, and I especially have -- I would note, Your Honour, that Defence counsel was warned or informed by the Prosecution two days ago that according to our information this is a photograph from 1993. This is not something that came up fresh in the course of the examination. Defence counsel chose to examine on this, made what we say are absolutely unsupportable comments about Mr. Galbraith's veracity under oath, and we think that he should publicly withdraw those comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I would imagine that that's logical. You can't in one breath accept the truthfulness of Witness Galbraith and at the same time call him a liar. In fact, even that comment can only be made at the time of argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, please. Mr. Black, before Mr. Milovancevic responds, just one small point. In his submissions to the Trial Chamber, I did not understand him to be saying that he accepted the truth of the statement. More he accepted the fact that the statement was made, after having been shown or read the record. So that was what I understood. Was he really accepting the truth of the statement which was made by Ambassador Galbraith from his submissions? I am following your other points, but on that one I don't see the basis for that submission of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There is a possibility that I have misunderstood the position. But as I was saying just before, we had alerted Defence counsel that this is -- actually, in fact, I am corrected. We didn't tell them it was 1993. We said it was a photo from before Storm, according to our information. We told them that two days ago. Then we discussed it over the break, and I understood him to be saying, okay, he accepted that this was not a photo taken during Storm. I'm looking for the cite, Your Honours. It's at page 30, line 16 he says: "I accept that this photograph is not from Operation Storm, because Ambassador Galbraith said he had never been atop a Croatian tank during Operation Storm." So based on that, that's what I was relying on for the fact that he accepted it was, as he said, not a photograph from Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite -- I agree to withdraw my comment on the answer of Witness Galbraith and I will keep it for argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you would allow me, I would like to continue questioning the witness, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's actually not the only reference. There was another reference a little later, which I would like you also to apply your mind to, if I can find it. Now, this is at line, the paragraph starting at line -- at page, sorry, page 31, line 24, to page 32, line 5. You said there, that's

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC SPEAKING
utterances.text: "Your Honour, Mr. Galbraith - and we can open this page 3851, line 5 and onwards - he did say he had never been atop a Croatian tank in Operation Storm. He was only on top of a tractor during Operation Flash, only a tractor, which shows that he denies he was never on a tank. And in further discussion when he was asked where he was at that moment, Mr. Galbraith explained that he was only on an armoured American vehicle." Maybe that's not -- doesn't absolutely require a retraction, but, okay, no, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the other citation that Your Honour may have had in mind is page 26, lines 17 to 20. And that's where Defence counsel said: "I asked -- I asked him were you atop a Croatian tank during Operation Storm, and he said no, now we see a photograph showing that, yes, he was." So I think that contradicts the position which has now been accepted and perhaps that's what Your Honour had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic, would you like to apply your mind to that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have that on my mind, but that does not need to be corrected, Your Honours, because the ambassador gave this statement, which I quote under this line 31, there is an explanation associated generally with this reference to the tank and the possibility for the ambassador to be atop it. The ambassador has given his explanation, of course, but I retracted this sentence which refers to the Storm operation because it is not a photograph from the Storm operation, and I have corrected, retracted my statement in that connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, line 19 at page 26, line 19 to 20 becomes unnecessary, if you accept that. Where you say "now we see a photograph showing that, yes, he was. I don't understand the problem." I think that statement becomes completely -- it contradicts what you had just said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all right, Your Honours. I accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Milovancevic, your statement now also includes page 25, line 19, and line 20, Mr. Galbraith having deceived the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that what Mr. Black referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was the first instance and then the second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He has is already withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, look at this photograph on the paper in front of you. Look at it well. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see, although it is quite small.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is in front of Mr. Galbraith, and you were a reserve officer yourself. There is something jutting in front of him.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a machine-gun on the top of the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Next to Mr. Galbraith, there is a man in uniform with glasses. Do you see him?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the right of him is a man without a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is right. But let us -- do let us pause between question and answer. In front of this man who is not wearing a cap --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask, for my elucidation, who is Mr. Galbraith of all the people that are on that photograph? I hear you talking of to his right there being a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Galbraith is the first person on the left of the photograph. To his right-hand side, looking from where we stand of course, to his left is this man wearing glasses without a cap. I don't know who that man is. But Mr. Galbraith is the first person on the left side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have another question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, please, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, there is a question which I must pose to you, and it arises out of the point of objection which was taken by Mr. Black, that you had accepted, in principle, the truth of the statement made by Ambassador Galbraith, that he was not on a tank during Operation Storm. Is that correct? Because if that is so, and you accept the answer which he gave in cross-examination, then you wouldn't have a right to controvert that evidence and that statement of his through your witness in putting an inconsistent position to your witness. Do you understand what I'm saying? If you accept the truth of the statement made by Ambassador Galbraith, then why are you leading evidence from this witness to controvert it? It is not regular. It's not permissible under the rules of examination and evidence. This is why I took the point earlier on that you had really, in your submissions, only admitted that the statement was made. You weren't accepting the fact of its truth, but you have confirmed to this Court that you are accepting the fact of the truth of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am dealing with this photograph not to controvert Mr. Galbraith's statement that he was not atop a Croatian tank during the Storm operation. I am trying to do something else right now. The witness has given us an answer to the effect that during the Geneva negotiations he was informed that America and Germany had approved an attack against the Krajina, which started on the next day. That is the Storm operation. This photograph is associated with the text which is on this page. I am only trying to point to what -- in referring to this photograph and seeking to establish that Mr. Galbraith is on a tank on this photograph, I am trying to come to a conclusion, to elicit a conclusion whether Mr. Galbraith is objective or partial, whether he has aligned himself with one of the sides, whether his treatment of both sides, the Croatian and the Serbian is the same. That is my only purpose. I am no longer at all dealing with that topic, whether what Mr. Galbraith said is correct or not. I believe that that has been clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: In fact, thank you. It seems as if I was pre-emptive, having heard you refer to Mr. Galbraith then. I accept your position now. Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we deal with my problem, Mr. Milovancevic? My problem had been, can we identify the personalities on the photograph. You see, the witness has referred to a person to the right and to the left of Mr. Galbraith. I need to know who is Mr. Galbraith. I notice that there is what looks like a face of a human being below the blazer of the person on the extreme left, and next to his blazer there is yet another person in what is -- looks like a camouflage uniform. And those are small inserts. But on the main picture I see four people. And then below the person that looks like a lady, in something that looks like a ring, I seem to see something that looks like a face of a human being. Now so in addition to the four who are in the main picture, I see, one, two, three other faces. So let's know who we are talking about so that the Chamber is clear. Who is Mr. Galbraith, first? Can we identify him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please explain to us who is Mr. Galbraith on this photograph? Would you point to a detail on him.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, these people in the foreground, and Mr. Galbraith is the first one on the left-hand side with a tie.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anybody else?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know any of the other people shown in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That will do. Thank you. This head on the right-hand side of the photograph, what you can see, there is a circle in the head. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This woman, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That might be a human head. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could it be a member of the crew of the tank? This man has something --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you are correct, he has a cap. It's probably the tank driver, because he's wearing this cap on his head. It is the tank driver; now I can see more clearly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is the tank driver? The person that looks like a woman is a tank driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a woman. This is a man with a cap, it looks like a hairdo. He has to wear such a protective cap while driving a tank, that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which person is that on the photograph are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you will allow me, perhaps it would be easiest if we put the photograph on the ELMO and the witness could show us with a pencil exactly what he is talking about, without us having to conclude what is left and what is right. Will the usher please assist us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please show to us Mr. Galbraith and tell us what head you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean point at it with my finger?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You will be given an implement.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This here is Mr. Galbraith. This here is Mr. Galbraith. So this person here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The one next to him in glasses, is that glasses?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The next one, next to him, in dark glasses to Mr. Galbraith's left? Who is that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are sitting, there up. He is not the driver. This is the driver, here. [Indicates]. But of course it is a very poor image, but that is the driver wearing this protective cap. It is not a lady's hairdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us who these people behind are? No, no, below. Here on the left.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, what I am showing right now, this is a soldier wearing a camouflage uniform, but of course this is not a clear enough image for us to be able to make out the details. We can see that it is a soldier in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why are these people down there? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably as security, as escorts, escorting these people riding on the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I meant why are they on a lower level in relation to Mr. Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they are not on the tank. They are behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said a while ago that you could see this machine-gun, where is it? Could you show it to us?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see the barrel here very nicely. Quite clearly. This is of course something that is used if there should be -- if the need should arise in case of some operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this photograph can be admitted, if the Trial Chamber does not have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The photograph is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, in connection with this photograph is also the text which is rounded. What date do you see in the bottom left-hand corner. Can we see the left-hand bottom corner of this page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, can we have an English translation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will just refer to the date, that is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not able to read the date in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: August 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- in B/C/S. Are you looking at the date at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: August 11th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, when I am talking to counsel --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just keep quiet, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Excuse me, Mr. Moloto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just keep quiet, please. You're not in a class here, okay, you're in a court. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. The date only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should also like to give you the reason for that. We showed you -- showed a page from the Daily Press which bears the date of the copy in question, and the date which is in the left corner is in the Cyrillic script and we shall translate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But I shall like to ask the witness what the date is.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the 11th of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 1995. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Just one thing before we move on. Perhaps we're about to go to this, but I'm a little confused about what is in evidence now. It was asked that the photograph be admitted into evidence. And then -- and that's fine that there is a reference to the date also on the same page. And if that's all that's gone into evidence, I'm fine. If the text is going to go into evidence, I might have an objection, because I really have no idea what it says, since we don't have a translation. So at this point I would object to the text going in, but the photograph and the date is just fine with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, as I understood Mr. Milovancevic, I asked him for the translation. He says it's -- from the photograph he is going to the date and date only, so I accept -- I would imagine, therefore, that what is admitted into evidence is the photograph and the date, and not the article. I see him nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
