utterances.text: The date being the date of the publication of the photo in the Serb newspaper, isn't it? Can we take that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for clarification then. In relation to the exhibit that is being admitted, the Chamber clarifies that only the photograph and the date of the newspaper are admitted into evidence and not the writings in B/C/S that are -- surround the photograph. Thank you very much. I hope the record makes it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Until when did you stay in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the Geneva accords, then I went to Martinbrod and I couldn't return to Knin because there was a big column of refugees heading for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 3rd in the evening you received from the Russian representative the information that the operation, Croatian operation was going to commence.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This operation began on the 4th of August at dawn. Since I had the information from the representative of the Russian mission -- excuse me. I cannot follow because of the interpretation. [In English] Sorry, I don't have the transcript on the screen. All right. Thank you. [Interpretation] Mr. Prijic, who was a member of the delegation, and myself addressed Mr. Peters, who was then a general, a Belgium general in the UNPROFOR forces, and who was with us in Geneva. We asked him to be able to return to Krajina as soon as possible. He just laughed. He said that they had their own schedule and there was no problem. They were aware of Operation Storm which had been prepared previously. Pavicevic, our ambassador to Geneva, also had this information, he told us that he would take us to Samaruga. This means that we were to request the help of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Pavicevic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pavicevic was the ambassador of Yugoslavia in Geneva, and he greeted us when we arrived to Geneva. We thought that we had come to negotiate and to settle certain issues, but as soon as the ambassador told us that he was taking us to Samaruga we realised that we would need assistance from the Red Cross, which we did not expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you need assistance of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because Operation Storm started on the next day and people were fleeing the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this brings me to the conclusion of this questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, my name is Mr. Black. I'm one of the Prosecutors in the case, and now it is my turn to ask you questions for a little while.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't want to ask you questions about history or about World War II. I don't want you to take that as an indication that I agree with you on your views on those matters, but I am going to try to focus on events in the 1990s, which are more directly relevant to these proceedings. And first I want to ask you a little bit about some activities as SAO Krajina minister of information in 1991. And the first thing I want to do is to clarify some dates. You testified that the first SAO Krajina government was established in December of 1990. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible, sir. However, I didn't think I had to write down everything that was going on. I don't think the dates are relevant. The events are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, for these purposes, I'll decide what's relevant, and if you can just try to answer my questions the best that you can. So do you think that -- you said yesterday that the first SAO Krajina government was established in December 1990. Is that still what you think today or would you like to change your testimony on that date, or do you just simply not remember the date?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall, sir, that I took an oath on St. Michael's Day, 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You would agree with me, wouldn't you, that you were the minister of information in the first SAO Krajina government. There wasn't another government before you became minister, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I would like to show you another document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could please see ERN 02195913. And the English is actually the next page, 02195914. If we could see those on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, I have a little bit of a problem. I'm not quite sure whether you are satisfied with the answer that you got. You said that you will decide what was relevant. And then you went on to say: "So do you think that -- you said yesterday that the first SAO Krajina government was established in December 1990. Is that still what you think today or would you like to change your testimony on that date, or do you just simply don't remember?" "I recall, sir, that it was St. Michael's Day, the 19th of December." I don't know whether it is the 19th of December, 1890, 1790 or 2090.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I understood him to mean 1990, but I will follow up with the witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, perhaps you understood His Honour Judge Moloto's question. When you referred to the 19th of December, what year were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 19th of December. I apologise, I don't recall. It could have been 1991. I remember when the Croatian constitution was adopted. The day before this adoption we had adopted some legal roles. I can only remember the substance, but I don't recall the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not trying to confuse you here. Yesterday you said December 1990. You have also referred to the Croatian constitution, which was adopted in December 1990. Is that when you had -- that's when you thought you recalled this first SAO Krajina government being established, right? And if you can just answer that, and then we will look at the document and we will see if we can clarify the dates.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't reply to this question. As far as the date is concerned, I apologise, but I never wrote the dates down, nor did I make an effort to remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you -- Your Honour, I think with my next few questions I can elucidate this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. And if you could elucidate on whether the Croatian constitution was also the day before this 1991 or 1990, whatever the date is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you have some trouble with dates and I accept that. The Croatian constitution, the so-called Christmas constitution, that was adopted in December of 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was the Christmas constitution and it was probably adopted in 1990 because this was when they won the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, does that satisfy you for the moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Macura, there is a document on your screen. This document is the decision electing you minister of information for the SAO Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And looking at the date of this document, you will agree with me, would you not, that that happened in May of 1991, not in December of 1990.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be made an exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm still on the update. Is that, this document 021? I beg your pardon. Document 02195914?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. The B/C/S is 02195913, and the English is 5914.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 943.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, just again to establish a little bit the dates. The parties in this case have agreed that the RSK was established in December of 1991. Does that sound right to you? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I apologise, but SAO Krajina, RSK, I think I got the dates confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about some of your own statements. Hopefully it will be easier to remember that. You believed, in 1991, and you publicly stated as minister of information, that all Serbs should live in a single Serb state. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could look at a document on the e-court, please. It's 06037135. I apologise, Mr. Macura. This is a news article that I only have in English. I don't have it in B/C/S, but I know that you read English very well, so hopefully it won't cause a problem. If we could just blow that up a bit, please. Mr. Macura, as you see here, this is a news article from the Financial Times dated the 3rd of August, 1991. You will see there in the first paragraph there is a reference to you, Lazar Macura. And then the second paragraph says -- it quotes you. It says: "All Serbs should live in a compact Serbia, said Mr. Macura, minister of information in the self-proclaimed Serb inhabited Autonomous Region of Krajina, south Croatia, which borders with Bosnia-Herzegovina." You did in fact say that in August 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you move down a couple of more paragraphs. There is one right next to a black dot that starts "Mr. Macura believes." It then says: "Mr. Macura believes a territorial corridor stretching from Krajina across Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbia is the obvious solution to uniting the two Serb communities." Now, there you're referring to the so-called Posavina corridor; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But if I may, sir, all the Serbs lived in one compact state until then and they should have remained in one state. They were not the ones asking for secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. If you could just focus on my question, please. I asked you if you were referring here to the so-called Posavina corridor. That's what you were referring to, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you considered that to be the obvious solution to uniting Krajina with not only the Serb inhabited parts of Bosnia but also with Serbia, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because I think the Serbs have this right of determination, self-determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you look at the last paragraph of this, before it gives the copyright information, et cetera, it says "he." And this is referring to you, Mr. Macura. It says: "He is adamant that no Serbian community in Yugoslavia should be categorised as a Serb minority. Yet when Franjo Tudjman, President of Croatia, this week offered cultural and political autonomy to the Serbs in Croatia, following repeated bombardment by Serb nationalists of Croat villages, the Serbs in Krajina were in no mood to accept the offer." And that paragraph is accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the conclusion of the journalist who wrote the article, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But it is correct, isn't it, that President Tudjman of Croatia offered cultural and political autonomy to the Croatian Serbs in early August 1991, but that offer was rejected by the leadership in Knin. True?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this. I don't remember Tudjman offering anything. They never wanted to negotiate with us. They only sent their police troops. They never wanted to negotiate with the politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please, if you could just try to answer my question. If it is necessary to add more information, I will ask you for more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document also be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 944.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, it was also your position as minister of information, that the Serbs in Krajina did not want to be part of an independent Croatia and that they in fact had the right to secede if Croatia seceded from Yugoslavia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I still hold that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could see another document on the screen, please. Actually, it is part of a larger document as it's been uploaded. The doc ID should be 03251158, and I'm actually interested in page 120 of that document, which has the ERN 03251277. And with the assistance of the usher, this is a document that's only in B/C/S. I was able to ask a colleague to do a draft translation. It is not an official translation, Your Honours, but it may help you follow along, so if I could distribute copies to Defence counsel and to the Bench, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Draft translation of the black document we see in front of us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Of one very, very small portion of it, Your Honour, and it is on page 120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could please on the B/C/S focus on the top right-hand corner of the document, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura you will see there there's a heading that refers to the 8th of August, 1991, Belgrade, Tanjug. And what this says -- it makes reference to an interview you gave to Austrian radio where you pointed out that there is a restoration of fascism in Croatia, and that Serbs do not want to be part of an independent state of Croatia and that they have the right to secede from that Yugoslav republic if she secedes from Yugoslavia. That was your position in August of 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence as well. And I will ask for an official translation of that excerpt, only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: In fact, it refers to the Tanjug report of the 7th August, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: At the same time to a source of the 8th, which may be an evening edition or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. I agree it's a little confusing, but that is the passage I'm focused on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It's the one at the very top?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, may I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain this, about the dates. Glas is a publication that was a monthly, so the date should not confuse you. It was not a newspaper. It was a monthly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the document please be admitted into evidence. I'm sorry we have sort of side-stepped you. I know that you wanted to tell us and that everybody jumped in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Your Honour this will become Exhibit number 945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, even in January of 1992, when the Vance Plan had been adopted, your position then was that the Krajina would never be part of Croatia again and that war would probably continue despite the Vance Plan. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And that's how it happened. But Krajina is nowadays a part of Croatia, although the war did continue there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me show you another news article, and this one bears the ERN 06037133. If we could -- again this is in English, Mr. Macura. If we could focus in just on the top third of the page, perhaps, that's fine. You will see that this is an Associated Press article dated 17th of January, 1992, from Knin. And you'll see there the second and third paragraphs. It's quoting you, it says: "Europe does not understand. We'll never be part of Croatia again, said Lazar Macura, Information Minister of the Krajina region of western Croatia." And then it quotes you some more. It says: "The war has not ended. This is only a brief timeout, said Macura." And that's a correct representation of your views as minister of information at that time, right, in January of 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not only my position, it was the position of those who elected me and the SDS of Krajina as a party, of Dr. Milan Babic as the president, and all the members of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but just focus on my question. Just answer my question, that will be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to ask the question. Mr. Macura, the article goes on to say: "A cease-fire between Serb-led forces and Croatian units has been in effect with sporadic violations for 15 days. Federal army and Croatian officials are optimistic it can hold. Not Macura. 'When the war starts again, it will only stop when one side exterminates the other,' he said." Was that your position also at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And that's what happened, and the Serbs were the side that lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this become Exhibit number 946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, may I ask you: These kind of statements were made by you because you were the minister of information, do I see this correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I had to act in accordance with the official policy of the government. I was not a freelancer making statements of his own accord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That was the gist of my question. Thank you very much. Please, Mr. Black, you may go on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, you mentioned there wasn't -- this wasn't just your position, it was also the position of some others, and you mentioned Milan Babic. Was it also Milan Martic's position at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in direct contact with Mr. Martic, because we were not doing the same job, but it's possible that he shared that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm a little confused. You're saying you don't know it was, or it was not, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could look at another document also from the 17th of January, 1992. It's ERN 06037134. As it is coming up, Mr. Macura, you told a reporter from the New York Times that the Serbs in Krajina would rather continue the war than to recognise Croatia's borders at that time as legal borders. Correct? Do you remember taking that position in January of 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that, sir, because international borders may not be changed according to the final Helsinki Act. They have to remain sovereign states. Otherwise, if you start with secessions, that can have no end. Those were internal borders, they cannot be international borders, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me focus you on -- if we could scroll down to the bottom of this article which again is in English. There you will see your name in bold. That paragraph says: "'Croatia has not had control here for over 18 months,' says Lazar Macura, Information Minister of the self-declared Krajina republic, speaking by telephone tonight from Knin, the centre of the Serb rebellion in Croatia." It continues to quote you: "We will go forward with the war before we will recognise the present borders as Croatia's legal borders." And that was your position in January of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before the Vance Plan was adopted, and insurgency broke out in Croatia vis-a-vis Yugoslavia before the insurgency in Knin, which means that the insurgency of Croatia against Yugoslavia preceded the insurgency in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me focus you again on my question. What I just quoted to you from this news article, that was your position on the 17th of January, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my position in January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 947.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, you mentioned earlier in your testimony that the Serbs in Croatia had initially demanded cultural autonomy. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. But that was at the very outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You remember that on the 25th of July, 1990, there was a Serb Assembly in Srb where there was actually a declaration adopted on this precise issue of autonomy; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I was not at that rally. I know it was held, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you a bit about the content of the declaration to see if you know that. The declaration is in evidence in this case. Under that declaration it said that the scope of Serb autonomy would have to depend on whether Croatia stayed in Yugoslavia, and specifically if Croatia remained in a federal Yugoslavia, then the Serbs demanded essentially cultural autonomy. But if Croatia separated itself from Yugoslavia, then the Serbs had the right, according to the declaration, to "political and territorial autonomy." That's correct, isn't it? That was the position in July of 1990?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So basically from the very beginning from July of 1990, the Serbs in Krajina were already contemplating the option of territorial autonomy from Croatia, which is another way of saying independence; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct that it was tantamount to independence. That was the kind of autonomy that was offered to us in Grac in 1993. We would have had the same status as the Tirol, but the Croats refused to continue those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say about the same status as Tirol, are you there referring to cultural autonomy or political autonomy or territorial autonomy? Which one of those is represented by Tirol in your view?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Tirol has also political autonomy, not only cultural autonomy within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. But it doesn't have territorial autonomy. That is something more, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it has political autonomy, which is significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: All right. Separate from that I'm focused on territorial autonomy. Tirol does not have territorial autonomy. That is something more, right? More than political autonomy.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Are you speaking of Tirol as part of Italy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tirol is either in Italy or in Austria. All I know is that we got the offer to have the same status as Tirol at one point. Some other options were mentioned, like islands of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear which islands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, these negotiations did not continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear which islands you are referring to. Can you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Oland islands; it is somewhere in Finland or Sweden. It doesn't matter. That was also on the table at one point. That's what matters. However, none of it was finalised. That's the tragedy. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one more question as to the issue of the status of Tirol. Who did offer that, and where? And when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was at a three-day meeting in Grac in 1993. There was Dr. Pupovac from Zagreb, Milos Vojnovic from Krajina, myself, and there was a Croatian delegation. And there were UN representatives as mediators. I don't know who organised the meeting. However, all that was discontinued later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. From whom the offer came, did you say that also? Do I have to understand you that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The representative of the United Nations proposed it. I don't remember the name of the man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could just look briefly at Exhibit 236 on our screens, please. Mr. Macura, this is a document that you were asked questions about by Defence counsel. It's from September of 1991. Do you remember that document, the one that says The Hague peace conference on Yugoslavia, on the top of it, do you remember discussing that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a million documents. I can't remember all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you if we can focus in perhaps on that first paragraph. If we could scroll down just a little bit, please. Thank you. Mr. Macura, just read that first paragraph to yourself and tell me if that refreshes your recollection, you remember talking about this document with Defence counsel earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed that this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn to the second-to-last page, just above the signature, please. I believe it is page 7. If we could focus in on the bottom, the last, the last two or three or four lines at the bottom of the page. That's fine. Now, Mr. Macura, the last sentence of this document signed by Milan Babic says: "To the Serb nation, being free means being sovereign. While being sovereign means existing in the form of one's own democratic state." That was Mr. Babic's position in September 1991, and it was your own position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think it is probably time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just before I go back to my questions. First, to clear up one thing about Exhibit 945. This was the one that I said was page 120 of a much larger document. It wasn't -- I went back and looked and it wasn't clear. We only asked for the particular page that we were interested in to be admitted into evidence, not the whole however many hundred pages it is. And so I will, if this works with the registrar, I will ask that we just take the large document out of e-court and just put the one page in e-court, so that it is clear what it is that we're relying on, if that is a solution that is acceptable to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If that is acceptable also and it's possible to registry? Thank you very much. So it is ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just one other thing about scheduling today. At the end yesterday the Trial Chamber had indicated that you wanted to go back to this issue of revised estimates. Should I leave some time for that at the end of the day today or how would you like me to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We would appreciate if you could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Should I leave about 15 minutes, Your Honour, or more or less? I'm at your disposal, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, these discussions usually take longer than they're supposed to. Leave as much as you possibly can without compromising your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is unlikely I will finish my cross-examination today, so it's just a question of when I stop, to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, we can deal with this issue after this witness is finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. However you prefer, Your Honour. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, sorry for the interruption while we talked about some other matters. I want to see if I understand your position on the changes to the Croatian constitution in December of 1990. I don't want to spend too much time on this but I just want to see if we can understand one another. Do you remember testifying a little bit about this yesterday, about why it was important that the Serbs' status in Croatia was changed from a constituent nation to a minority. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Prosecutor, I shall try to be brief and to explain the essence of the issue to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, actually you explained it yesterday, and I just want to ask a couple of questions about what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First of all, well, so that there is no confusion. Yesterday at transcript 28 to 29, you were asked about this specific issue, and let me read out to you what you said so you have in mind what you said yesterday. You say: "We thought that we would never be divested of the status of a constituent people." "That we could never be divested," excuse me, "of the status of a constituent people. But this was violence against law, because Croatia could not unilaterally divest us of that status." We would have -- "We were supposed to be asked." "And secondly, it is true that -- the second factor is that Croatians announced that they would secede from Yugoslavia, and we thought that we had the -- that the pre-emptive right of remaining in the country of our birth, and that that right pre-empted the right of secession from that country. We had no claims to Croatian towns in which many Serbs lived, but we did have a compact territory which could have been completely separated from Croatia in the way that Croatia was separated from Yugoslavia. There, the population were 80 per cent Serbs. In the area of Knin, Croats accounted for only 7 per cent, whereas now there are no Serbs there at all." That's what you said yesterday, Mr. Macura.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is it your view that Croatia could not change the constitutional status of Serbs, nor secede from Yugoslavia without first obtaining the agreement of the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is only normal for me, because we participated in the creation of Croatia, both in the First and in the Second World War, and Serbs had the most casualties in both world wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let's not -- let's not talk about World War II right now anyhow. I'm not sure you answered my question. Is it your view that Croatia couldn't change the constitutional status of Serbs, nor could it secede from Yugoslavia without first obtaining the agreement of the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my position, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So, in other words, the Serbs had a kind of veto power over Croatian secession and this kind of important constitutional change, or important in your view anyhow.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all previous Croatian constitutions, the Serbs were an equal people in Croatia, and that is why I think the Serbs should have also been asked, rather than have the constitution amended unilaterally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, my question is a little bit different. It's not about what you think should have happened, but did you think that Croatia could not change that status and could not --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- without the agreement first?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is what I thought. That is what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So it's not only a question of what they should have done but what they could do, what their possibilities were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You mean legal possibilities, or moral possibilities or historical obligations? Maybe you can ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, you heard Judge Hoepfel's question, and maybe it was to me. But are you speaking of legal possibilities, moral possibilities or historical possibilities? Or obligations?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legal, moral and historical, whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday in the part that I read out about a compact territory which could have been completely separated from Croatia. And there you were referring basically to the Krajina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you mentioned about the numbers of -- you had some figures about how many Serbs and Croats you thought composed the population in Krajina. In your view, what would have happened to the Croats living in Krajina if Krajina separated itself from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were ready to give the Croats all rights as to Serbs, to treat them on an equal footing as the Serbian people. So nothing would have happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, isn't that exactly what Croatia guaranteed for the Serbs, that they would have all rights guaranteed to them?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it abolished our basic right, the right of a constituent people. And from that emanated many other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you saying that -- well, what do you mean when you say "we were ready to give the Croats all rights as to Serbs." What rights are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were prepared to treat them as an equal people, a people living side by side with the Serbian people. They were in the minority, but President Babic kept repeating that nothing could happen to the Croats inside of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you talking about -- when you say "treat them as an equal people," do you mean that they would have been a constituent nation of the Krajina? Or that they would have been a minority whose rights were protected?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that issue would be treated by the constitution later, when it was adopted. But Mr. Prosecutor, if you will allow me to explain. In the Knin Krajina, we did nothing to the Croats, inflicted no evil on them during the war. I'm referring to this latest war, not to the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I will ask you some questions about that later, but that's not my focus right now. Could we please see Exhibit 137 on the screen. Mr. Macura, you told us yesterday that you were -- you held public office as a member of the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What you see on the screen in front of you is the founding document of the SDS from the 17th of February, 1990, in Knin. Were you present at that founding Assembly of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present, Mr. Prosecutor. I only joined later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If I could ask you to look at the last page. It's the last page in English and the last page in B/C/S original. Mr. Macura, you can see on the screen now in front of you, this is the SDS resolution on Kosovo, which was adopted at this February 1990 Assembly. And if you focus on the second-to-last paragraph down there, near the bottom of the page, if we could scroll down, please. And it says in that paragraph, this is the SDS resolution speaking: "We advocate that the Albanians should keep those rights which minorities in most democratic countries of the world have. We are in favour of them holding all the rights they have. There is no minority in the world which has its academy of sciences, its universities, its independent national school curriculum, it's independent media, including radio, television and publishing houses. They have everything but a state. We are vigorously against two Albanian states in the Balkans of which one would be created in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Serbia." And my question, sir, is that the SDS had a double standard, didn't it? It thought that Albanians in Kosovo should have --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me finish my question and then you will have a chance to respond. The SDS --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's okay. The SDS thought that Albanians in Kosovo should be content with minority rights, but that Serbs in Croatia should have some further rights, some special status. Right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, can I explain to you something which I know from my personal experience, and I shall be very brief. Krajina is ethnically and historically a Serbian land and Kosovo is only ethnically Albanian. Mr. Mustajbasic from Belgrade, who was -- is a retired diplomat, was in Djakovica in 1946. And he told me: I spent six months in Djakovica. That is a town on the border between Kosovo and Albania. There were 10.000 Albanians from Albania crossing that border, crossing monthly, entering Kosovo in order to remain living in Kosovo. And Josip Broz prohibited Serbs from returning to Kosovo by a law. In that way Albanians became the ethnic majority, even after the death of Josip Broz. The president of the state was an Albanian from Albania, he was Fadil Hoxha. He did not have Yugoslav citizenship but he was the president of Yugoslavia, is the president of the collective leadership in Belgrade. So, I believe, Mr. Prosecutor, that these are two completely different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, my first question is: So you say that Albanians have no historical claim to Kosovo, dating beyond 1940s? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. If you find a single Albanian monument in Kosovo -- I'm talking in historical terms and that can't be done because there never have been any, I will give you whatever you ask for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, I suppose you realise that many Albanians in Kosovo see that issue very differently and feel that the Albanian people in Kosovo do have a historical claim.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite normal. You're probably right there, but I'm just talking -- telling you what the historic facts are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you're really telling me what your version of the historic facts are, because other people may have their own version of the historic facts; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, history can be falsified and interpreted in whatever way one pleases, but I gave you the statement of a man whom I talked to who is not a Serb. He's a Muslim from Belgrade. He was a diplomat and he spent those six months at the Djakovica border crossing. And I do like to quote people who are not Serbs, lest it seem as propaganda. What I'm saying, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What is that person's name?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mustajbasic. He lives on Rimska Street near the Hotel Serbia, and I talked to him on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And according to you, what this person says that he saw in the town of Djakovica establishes the true historic facts for all of Kosovo. That's what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because the Serbs were prohibited from returning to Kosovo by law. They could not return to their homes, to their estates, just like I myself am unable to return to Croatia now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's good that you mention Croatia. Let me focus back on Croatia. You would also accept, wouldn't you, that some Croatians have a different view from you about the history of Krajina, that they would say that Krajina historically also pertains to the country of Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'll tell you that one just need look in the registry books, the real estate registry to see whose the land is. That was during Austria, Venice, the Turkish empire. Just consult the land registry books and you will see whom the land belongs to. But that this is not even good for the Croats, Mr. Prosecutor. This is now a wasteland, it is an empty space. It is not good for the Croats either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I guess the point that I'm driving at is that people have different views about historical claims. And so history, historical claim to a land can't be the basis for deciding about issues of secession and constitutional rights, can it? Because people are never going to agree on that.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Prosecutor, but here the Helsinki Accords on the inviability of external borders has been violated, but only on the example of Yugoslavia. I don't see why it doesn't apply to all other countries then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we're done with that document, please. It can be taken off the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, at several points in your testimony yesterday you mentioned Branimir Glavas. Do you remember that, do you remember talking about him?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember. And I remember him from television. I saw him on television a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: He is an extreme right wing Croatian nationalist, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And as you also mentioned yesterday, he's currently being investigated for war crimes in Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it is very protected exercise and the witnesses are actually refusing to take the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about some details and see what you know about the actual proceedings against Mr. Glavas. Specifically, Glavas is accused of arresting and torturing two Serbs and then ordering them shot in Osijek; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details. I know that -- what I do know is that many Serbs were killed in Osijek and Glavas was man number 1 of the Croatian Democratic Union in Osijek. So if the Croats think him responsible, he probably is. What I also do know is that he threatened Radoslav Tanjga as he was speaking in the Croatian parliament, that is our representative. He was threatening him with a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You said yesterday and you kind of I think alluded to this here that you thought Croatia was dragging its feed in the proceedings against Glavas. Right? Is that how you feel about it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have that feeling, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that in May of 2006, that's May of this year, the Croatian parliament lifted Glavas's parliamentary immunity specifically in order to facilitate the current investigation of him.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but that is ten years after the Storm operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You probably also didn't hear, then, that he actually appealed that decision, but the Zagreb Court of Appeals rejected his request and an official judicial inquiry was opened in July of 2006. Does that ring a bell to you at all?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not following it. I am no longer interested in him. I am in exile from the Krajina, I cannot go back to it anymore, so I really am not following that sphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm just asking you questions about it because you yourself mentioned it. As far as you know, his trial is expected to begin either later this year --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I just remembered. I remember him, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a couple of more questions about it. As far as you know, his trial is expected to begin either later this year or in -- early in 2007; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know that if he's convicted he faces 15 to 20 years in prison?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have my doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: About what do you have your doubts?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my doubts about that, that he will be given a sentence, Glavas that is, of between 15 and 20 years of imprisonment. But seeing is believing, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Seeing is believing. Why do you doubt it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt it because of the fact that the Croatian public has different feelings about it and about this law and the possible punishment to be meted out to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're aware, aren't you, that there are other war crimes cases proceeding in Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There certainly are, but I'm really not following that because I'm not really interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Have you heard anything about the Lora prison case from Split? Do you know anything about that case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What case, once more?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The Lora, L-o-r-a, prison case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I followed Lora during the war. I know that Serbs were tortured there, not only Serbs from the Croatian Krajina but also Serbs from Bosnia, namely from another state. And I know that there was a trial, that it was discontinued and later resumed, but I didn't follow it from that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that -- you're quite right that there was a trial. They were found not guilty, but then that was overturned on appeal. And at the re-trial, which lasted five and a half months, two Croatians received sentences of eight years in prison, another, a military policeman, Croatian, was sentenced to seven years in prison, and five other Croatians were given six-year terms for their role in the beating and torturing of civilians. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but it is quite all right that something should be done along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you testified yesterday about -- you just mentioned about Sisak and things that you say happened in Sisak. In fact, you testified that in Sisak "Serbs were killed at every step." That non-Croats were "rounded up and killed for no reason at all." "And that anyone from Sisak will tell you that they know at least 50 Serbs killed in Sisak." My question for you is: Where did you learn this information? What's your source for this information?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Nikola Dobrijevic who is from Sisak and now lives in Belgrade. He knows of many Serbs who were killed. He knows their names, they would come to their workplace, to sign some declarations, and then they were shot in the back of the head. That's what he told me. I have no reason not to believe him. I also know some other people from Sisak whose family members are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So besides Mr. Dobrijevic, do you know any Serbs -- actually, do you know any one from Sisak who can talk to you about other Serbs that were killed there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a student in high school whose father was killed. He was also from Sisak. I was born far away from Sisak. I don't know the region that well. But I heard this information and I know that Nikola Dobrijevic has a lot of information on that, because he lived in Sisak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And when precisely do you say these things happened?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They happened during the war. There were no combat activities in Sisak and this is what I would like to turn your attention to. There were no combat activities in Sisak, and nevertheless there were killings. I cannot give you the exact period, the duration, but I'm sure that you will have an opportunity to get evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you even give us the year, maybe, in which you say these things happened? Or the range of years?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I really don't have an interest in dates or years. The only thing I'm interested in is what happened and the status that I'm at now. I was defeated in a war. I cannot return to my place of birth, and I have no other interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I hope you can appreciate that for the job that we have to do here, we are interested in dates. So if you don't know a date, you can tell me that. But I'm going to continue at times to ask you about dates --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- and I would ask you to do your best.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who killed these people, as far as you know, the Serbs who you say were killed in Sisak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed by their co-workers, by Croats who lived in the same town. But of course the authorities were to blame and the power was held by the Croatian Democratic Union, because it is impossible for people to be killed or hurt without the knowledge of the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You know, when we first started talking about this, I think you said that people were killed when they came to work. Is that right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the offices they were killed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You know, yesterday you said that non-Croats were "rounded up and killed." Do you have any examples of that, of people being rounded up and killed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard on the news, but this was not confirmed later on, so I cannot claim that it actually happened. But anyway, near Spacvanska forest, I'm referring to the withdrawal of forces in the course of Operation Storm when the Serbian forces withdrew in a column as refugees headed towards Serbia, there were around 10.000 people in this group --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, because I think maybe we're talking at cross-purposes. Are you still talking about Sisak? Because I'm interested in what you said were crimes against Serbs in Sisak. Do you know of any cases where Serbs in Sisak were rounded up and killed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard some stories. There were some of them that they were thrown into furnaces in the Sisak plant, ironworks. This is what I heard. And in fact this is how this crime was left without any tracks. I cannot confirm that. I didn't see it. These were stories that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But is that what you meant when you said that Serbs or non-Croats were rounded up and killed? Is that what you were referring to, that they were burned in ovens?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that these were mass killings. Not individual cases. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what I am putting to you, sir, and my point in these questions is that you were pretty loose in the way you talked about what happened in Sisak, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was loose because I was not present there myself. I was not an eye-witness, so I think that this can be confirmed by the people who were eye-witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you were just repeating what you had heard, and you don't really know first-hand what happened in Sisak, do you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I don't know first-hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you don't really know, although you testified this way, you don't really know about people being rounded up and killed for no reason, do you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure. I can only relate what I was told, that many Serbs were killed in Sisak. Many. I don't know the exact numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Because yesterday you said that anyone from Sisak will tell you that they knew at least 50 Serbs who were killed there. But that was just a number you threw out there. That's not a number that you can backup with anything, is it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that Sisak is not a big town. And among the refugees from Serbia whose relatives were killed, they know exactly which people are no longer alive, and which people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any idea how many people, how many Serbs were actually killed in Sisak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard a figure of 250. I don't know if this is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First of all, what time-period approximately? You said you have trouble with dates. But approximately what time-period are you talking about that you heard 250 Serbs were killed in Sisak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was during the war. But as I said, there were no combat activities in Sisak and yet people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And from whom did you hear this figure of 250 Serbs killed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it from several people. I don't know their names. I can give you the name of Nikola Dobrijevic who can give you the exact names, if he testifies. I don't know if he is a witness before this Court or if he will be summoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You know you also testified about Serbs being killed in Zagreb. Do you remember talking about the Zec family?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, a film was made about this, Pavilion 22 I believe was the name. The Croats filmed this. The film about how Serbs were executed. So if the Croats made the film themselves, then it seems that they are willing to confess that crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you would please just wait for my questions then you will know what I'm going to ask you about instead of kind of giving speeches. My question is: Three people, three members of the Zec family were killed, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible. I know that the whole family was killed. I think perhaps one of the children survived. I don't remember the details, but this was written down and published.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you don't know any other examples of Serbs killed in Zagreb, do you, during the war?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, but others do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me change topics now and ask you about something different. I would like to focus your attention on the summer of 1990. And you told us yesterday that some policemen in Knin had refused to wear a new insignia that was introduced by the Croatian authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And by that you were referring to the chequer-board, that red-and-white chequer-board, right, that's the insignia you meant?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The insignia that you could see on the photograph where the Ustasha is holding the head. The decapitated head.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what does that insignia look like? I don't remember the photograph exactly.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the photograph today. The person who was standing next to Ambassador Galbraith wore it on his cap. It was a chequer-board in the shape of a letter U.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In the shape of a letter U or in the shape of a shield, right? That's like a crest, that's the shape you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, right. You are saying a shield. I'm saying it's U-shaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, that same symbol, with the same shape that you call a U shape, that was a Croatian symbol of Croatian kings since the middle ages, wasn't it, that chequer-board with that same U shape.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which kings you're referring to. There are legends and there are historical facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: All right. Well let me ask you about something. Do you agree with me that the Kingdom of Yugoslavia is a historical fact, right? That existed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it existed, and it was established thanks to Serbian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And its coat of arms included this same red-and-white chequer-board with what you call a U shape. That was part of the coat of arms of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know that the same chequer-board and the same U shape was part of the coat of arms of the People's Republic of Croatia and then formerly -- subsequently the Socialist Republic of Croatia during the entire time that Croatia was part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is repetition. Even the money, the currency that was introduced by Ante Pavelic was reintroduced, the kuna.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you right there because I'm not talking about Ante Pavelic. I'm not talking about the kuna. I'm asking you about this chequer-board and whether it was just, do you know, yes or no, or you don't know, that it was part of the coat of arms of Croatia when Croatia was republic of the SFRY, of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the seals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And so then you would agree with me that the independent state of Croatia and the Ustashas, they weren't the creators of this chequer-board symbol. They were simply one of several governments over history who incorporated that into their own symbolism, right, you would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They changed the insignia. I don't recall which insignia they used, but I know that they changed it, and that's why the police refused to accept a new insignia, new symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who changed it? You say: "They changed the insignia. I don't recall which insignia they used." Who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities in Zagreb. The new Croatian government led by the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So then I guess you haven't really answered my question which was that the NDH and the Ustashas, they didn't invent the chequer-board symbol. They were simply one of several governments over time that incorporated that into their own symbolism, right? Just answer that question.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that many Serbs were slaughtered by soldiers wearing this insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question, have you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't think you have answered my question, which is: Isn't it true that the NDH and the Ustashas did not invent or create this chequer-board symbol. They were simply one of several governments, over history, that incorporated that into their own symbolism. Please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and they abused it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And yet you considered this solely or primarily an Ustasha symbol. In fact, you even said it is in the shape of a U, rather than the shape of a crest. That's the way you saw this symbol, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a statue in the Jasinovac camp there was a flower which was also U-shaped. This was done on purpose, so it could be a memorial to the victims of the Serb, victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, it was really the U, that was really the most recognisable specifically Ustasha symbol, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only that, they wanted to change the uniforms. And I don't know the details, but I'm sure you can get this information from the people who were in the police forces. Who know more about uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You talked -- kind of following from this same issue, you mentioned yesterday of a letter from some policemen in Knin to the federal authorities objecting to the new insignia. Do you remember talking about that letter?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know this letter was drafted, and it was published in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: One of the people who signed that letter was Milan Martic, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you say "probably." You know that to be the case, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any details about this matter. I'm not a policeman. I had other duties. I know of the existence of this letter, and I know that it was published in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And in all the time that you were a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, it's a very simple question. Do you know or don't you know whether Martic was a co-author of this letter? If you don't know, there is no crime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- if he was the co-author or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So, Mr. Macura, in all the time that you were ministers together in a government and the time that you spent as a colleague of Mr. Martic, he never -- it never came up in conversation. You don't know one way or the other whether he was one of the people who signed that famous letter in July 1990?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never discussed it with him. Mr. Martic had many other obligations. We didn't meet very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I understand what you're saying, that you never discussed this letter with him. You say you didn't meet very frequently. You were ministers in the same government together, weren't you, in the SAO Krajina government?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but I had other duties to attend to. I was the general manager of the radio, and I was a minister on a voluntary basis. Free of charge. I was never paid for this. Each of us had other jobs and we performed these ministerial functions on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Even before May of 1991 when you became a minister in the SAO Krajina government, I take it you had contact with Mr. Martic before that date as well, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him only sporadically.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You were vice-president of Knin municipality in 1990, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But Mr. Martic was in the police forces, and there wasn't much connection with the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware that around the 5th of July, 1990, Croatian authorities, high-level Croatian authorities, including the Minister of Interior, Josip Boljkovac, and also I believe his deputy, Perica Juric, came to Knin to meet with Martic and other police who had signed that petition? Are you familiar with that meeting, the beginning of July 1990?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was when they came to the police station and people rallied around, there was a spontaneous rally. I'm not sure if you're referring to this event. I remember on one occasion that people rallied around the police station. Are you referring to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. That's the time -- that's the occasion that I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this. I was present there, together with other people in the street. I remember it. But I was not inside the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You say that people spontaneously gathered at the police station. In fact, that was kind of -- it was an organised effort to get people out to show support for their policemen, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that the Croatian authorities actually needed protection in order to be able to leave that meeting unharmed? They had to be kind of escorted from the building?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is probably so, and I think they were escorted. Nobody was hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And it was really from that point onward that Milan Martic and other policemen in Knin, at least, believed that the Croatian authorities had no further authority in Knin, right? From that point on, that was the belief, that Croatia had no authority there.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, in terms of the police, the way they were thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And specifically that's what Milan Martic, that was his position, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim this. Perhaps it was his position, but I don't know. I never asked him. You're probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever see on TV this famous statement where Milan Martic tells a Croatian journalist that the police in Knin was the people's police and that they don't listen to the Croatian government anymore? That was some time in August 1990. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen it, but I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And did you hear that that was what he said, that basically "they don't listen to the Croatian authorities anymore in Knin?"

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he mentioned the chequer-board.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That was actually a different statement. Did you hear about the statement where he said -- yeah, I understand the confusion. I will ask you now about that chequer-board. He made kind of a famous speech where he said as long as he lives the Croatian chequer-board won't be shown in Knin, or words to that effect, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And was that the one that you said that you didn't see but that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, I'm going to show you a quick video clip on the Sanction, if we could move to the Sanction, please. It is Exhibit 4. The transcript is actually marked Exhibit 5, but ... Please just watch along, Mr. Macura.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, did you ever see that --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it now. I see Mr. Martic, and the journalist is Heni Erceg who studied with me at the University of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know who -- I'm sorry, I didn't catch her name, but do you know who the woman was working for at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: She came with TV Split, Croatian Television from Split. And we studied together at the university. I can see that it was her on the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, it was also your view that Croatian authorities essentially lost control or had no more authority in Knin after the summer of 1990, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: During your evidence yesterday, the Defence counsel asked you whether the federal or the Croatian authorities ever did anything towards a peaceful solution of this issue regarding the new insignia. And you said that the federal authorities tried, but that "the people in Croatia would not listen to anything."

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, many things were done to reach some kind of peaceful solution from the federal level. But since the Croats had decided to secede from Yugoslavia, they were doing -- they were taking action which had nothing to do with the federal state. Or the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just because I think you're getting ahead of me. I'm still really just focused on, let's say, August/September of 1990. You know, when -- this meeting that we discussed, where there are people gathered outside of the police station and the Croatian authorities came to meet with Mr. Martic and others, that was -- that was an attempt by the Croatian authorities to peacefully deal with the situation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not share your opinion. I disagree. I think that the right way would have been to talk to politicians who had won the elections and not to discuss matters only with the police. But the politicians did not want to talk to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, this particular issue was a police issue, right, because it was the police in Knin who refused to wear the new police insignia, and so it made sense that Croatia would send the minister of interior, who headed the police, to try to work out this issue. And he tried to do so peacefully in July of 1990, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a much wider issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me, then, I guess, move to something just slightly wider. On the 10th of September, 1990, Milan Babic signed an agreement with officials from the Croatian -- of course Milan Babic was a politician. And he signed an agreement with Croatian officials to peacefully resolve the outstanding issues and even to return weapons that had been taken in August of 1990. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
