utterances.text: Perhaps we could see Exhibit 180 on the e-court, please. Mr. Macura, it's a little hard to read, I understand that, this document.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. I can read. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is basically a public announcement of this agreement that I just mentioned to you between Mr. Babic and others on the Serb side and Josip Boljkovac and others on the Croatian side. Have you ever seen this announcement before?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm seeing it now for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you see Mr. Babic's signature down at the bottom near his name?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, I do. I see all the signatories.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you -- you never, despite your close association with Milan Babic, you never heard about this agreement in September of 1990?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, sir. Never. Although I was at Mr. Babic's side wherever he went, always.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, apparently wherever he went except when he went to negotiate this agreement, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not mean at the local level. I had to accompany him at all his talks with the international community. Otherwise, I would stay behind in Knin whenever he went around travelling locally, because I was his deputy. So I could not follow him at those talks, because I had to work at the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- did you never hear that this agreement was actually rejected by the Council of National Resistance, and Milan Babic was even accused of being a traitor for having signed it. You never heard about that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me focus your attention for a moment on August of 1990, specifically on the 17th of August, 1990, and a few days, I guess, before or after that. You testified yesterday that the Croatian authorities moved to seize weapons from police stations in Benkovac and Obrovac in order to prevent the Serb referendum.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Obrovac. No. They removed weapons only in Benkovac. In Obrovac they didn't succeed because the people came out in the streets and stopped them. They did it only in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. They attempted to do it in Obrovac but it wasn't successful. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you said yesterday that the reason for those attempts to seize police weapons was to prevent the Serb referendum, right? That was what you said?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: According to you, then, local Serbs erected barricades in response to those, let's say, operations by the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My first question is that, you know, the weapons, the weapons which were seized were reserve police weapons, right? That's what was seized from Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the arsenal of the reserve police, but there were Serbs among the reserve policemen and not only Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. But that was the arsenal of the reserve police in Benkovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it should have been in Benkovac. It shouldn't have been removed, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But those weapons, they belonged to, they were the property of the Croatian MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That maybe correct, I don't know anything about ownership. But I know that there existed reserve policemen who were responsible for some weapons, because they had been issued with those weapons, and they should have stayed in Benkovac at their disposal. They should not have been removed and taken away God knows where. That means that practically the reserve police were disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My question -- you know, you say you don't know anything about ownership, but you don't really dispute, do you, that -- I mean, those were police weapons. And so when the Croatian MUP went to, as you say, seize those weapons, they were only taking control of what was in fact already theirs. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who do you say those weapons belonged to, if they didn't belong to the Croatian MUP?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reserve policemen were listed. There was no doubt as to who reserve policemen were, and it was exactly known what kind of weapons they had been issued with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So those weapons were issued to a certain number of reserve policemen, and every policeman was responsible for his own weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. The policemen may have been responsible in a sense for those weapons. But it's just like in the army, right, all the weapons of an army, whether it be guns or tanks, that doesn't belong to the soldiers. It belongs to the army. And in the same way, these weapons belong to the Croatian MUP. Right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that had been so, the SFRY would still exist today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So are you saying that that was not so?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand you. Are you saying that those weapons did not actually belong to the Croatian MUP? They belonged to someone else? Or to no one?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the weapons belonged to those who were responsible, in the sense that they had been issued with those weapons. What happened instead was the weapons were taken away from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So according to you, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to find out from the witness who had issued these weapons to this reserve people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their superiors, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who were their superiors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who they were, inspectors, or whatever. At any rate, there were some sort of superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would their superiors have the right to take them back from them, for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the point is that they had the intention to disarm the reserve police, and they had been threatening all the time that they were going to ban the referendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. Would their superiors have the right to take them back? I think you should be able to say yes or no, or you don't know. That's the only appropriate answer you can give.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So just so I understand, Mr. Macura. You're saying that you don't know whether the police arsenal in Benkovac belonged to the police, the Croatian police, the Croatian MUP. You just don't know?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the Croatian operations to take control of those police weapons, they were about taking control of weapons. They weren't about preventing a referendum. They were about taking control of weapons, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, do you really think that the Croatian MUP couldn't have prevented the referendum by force, if that's what they were after, instead of actually going and seizing weapons which belonged to them from specific police stations in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you think that by seizing weapons from Benkovac they were -- how is it that you think that that was an attempt to stop the referendum? Was Benkovac the only place where the referendum was going to be held?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think their intention was to do that, in all municipalities under our control, under the control of our authorities. So the intent was to do it in all municipalities, and when they failed in Obrovac, they gave up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You make a reference to municipalities under your control. I mean, isn't it the case that the Croatian police wanted to take control of these weapons because -- precisely because they were located in places where the local police were hostile to the Croatian government? They wanted to take control of those weapons so that the local police wouldn't use them against the Croatian government. Isn't that what the operations at Benkovac and the failed operation at Obrovac were really about?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certain that they intended to take control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But my question to you really was that -- the reason that they needed to control or felt they needed to control those weapons was precisely because the local police were hostile to the Croatian authorities. It wasn't about the referendum. It was about making sure that reserve police weapons weren't misused by local police who were against the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had hinted and stated enough times that they were going to stop the referendum. The Croatian authorities made no bones about it, and I stand by that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me move on to something related but slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I am going to move to a new subtopic and perhaps it's -- it makes more sense to stop today rather than risk going a couple of minutes over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that is more sensible to do that. Thank you very much. We have come to the end of the day today. The case is postponed until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of September, 2006, at 9.00 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.42 p.m.,
